name: Pūrṇa
sub: three ways to hold the infinite
description: The Upaniṣadic whole, the Jaina classes of number, and Bhāskara II's khahara.
aria: An endless spiral zoom into a mandala that contains itself
intro: Indian thinkers wrote about the infinite long before set theory. This chamber shows three of their ideas: a whole that stays whole, numbers too large to count, and division by zero.
legend: I: the mandala, containing itself at every scale
II: rings of seeds, ×10 each ring
III: 1 ÷ x as x slides to 0
III: khahara, the quantity divided by zero

tutorial.b: An old verse says that taking the whole from the whole leaves the whole. This picture contains itself forever.
Jaina thinkers sorted numbers into ones you can count, ones too large to count, and infinite ones. Each ring here holds ten times the last.
As x shrinks to 0, 1 ÷ x grows without limit. Bhāskara II called a number divided by zero khahara.
His rule was that adding to khahara does not change it. Modern set theory has a similar rule: adding a few items to an infinite set does not change its size.

sound:
Each movement has its own rule. I, pūrṇa: every note is Sa in a different octave, the same whole at a different scale. II, Jaina: the notes count up the scale, ten to a ring, then start again an octave… the counting never ends. III, khahara: one note that never changes, whatever is added around it.

Switching movement rings a bowl on harmonic 2, 3 or 4 of Sa (× 2, × 3, × 4), the first rungs of the infinite overtone ladder inside every note.

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: From the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1: that is whole, this is whole; from the whole the whole arises; taking the whole from the whole, the whole remains. It's a spiritual statement, but it describes infinite sets well.
In log coordinates the pattern repeats every time the radius grows by 3.2, with a twist of one full turn per repeat, so the rings fuse into one endless spiral.
Jaina texts class numbers as saṅkhyāta (enumerable), asaṅkhyāta (innumerable) and ananta (infinite), with several kinds of infinity: in one direction, two, an area, everywhere, perpetually.
Bhāskara II's name, in the Bījagaṇita (1150), for a quantity with zero as its divisor. Adding or subtracting doesn't change it.

faq.q: how does this relate to modern math?
faq.a: Cantor (1870s–90s) showed infinite sets can have equal size to their parts and come in different sizes. Today 1/0 is left undefined; what Bhāskara's rule anticipates is cardinal arithmetic, where ℵ₀ + n = ℵ₀.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'glow 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
